lead: Two tasks in this chapter look different and share one shape. Question answering takes a question and a passage and returns an answer — either a span copied from the passage or a sentence a model writes. Textual entailment takes a premise and a hypothesis and returns one label: entailment, contradiction or neutral. Both feed two texts into a single encoder and read a decision off the joint representation. Search engines, bank chatbots, helpline desks and fact-checking tools use them. This chapter gives the pipeline, the labels, and the two numbers that score question answering.
prereq: You need: BERT fine-tuning and the [CLS] vector from 6.4, and named entity recognition for entity-type answers from Unit 2.

sections.h3: Two texts in, one decision out

blocks.text: Question answering and textual entailment are both sentence-pair tasks. One text is the question or the premise; the second is the passage or the hypothesis. The model reads both and produces a small output — a span, a generated sentence, or one label out of three.

The recipe is the one from 6.4. Join the two texts into one sequence with a separator token between them. Run the encoder. Read the decision from the joint representation — either the [CLS] vector at the front or the per-token vectors of the second text.

Sharing one encoder is why these two tasks are taught together. The engineering is the same work every time: tokenise a pair, pad to one length, fine-tune, evaluate. Only the output head and the label set change.

A factoid question wants a short answer: a name, a date, a number. "Who wrote the national anthem of India?" wants a person. If you know the expected answer type in advance, named entity recognition from Unit 2 can filter candidate answers.

In open-domain QA no passage is supplied. The system runs in two stages — retrieval, then reading. The retriever ranks passages from a large collection against the question (see 6.8). The reader then looks inside the top few passages only.

In reading comprehension the passage is given and the answer is usually a span copied out of it. SQuAD is the standard benchmark of this kind: people wrote questions against Wikipedia paragraphs and marked the answer as a character range inside the paragraph.
Generative QA drops the span constraint. A large language model from 6.5 writes the answer in its own words, and those words may appear nowhere in the passage.

sections.h3: The extractive reader: score a start and an end

blocks.text: An extractive reader treats the answer as a pair of positions in the passage. For every passage token the model produces a start logit and an end logit.
P_start(i) = softmax over passage tokens of (w<sub>s</sub> · h<sub>i</sub>)
blocks.where: h<sub>i</sub> is the encoder output vector at passage token i; w<sub>s</sub> is a learned weight vector; the softmax runs across all passage tokens; P_end(j) uses a second vector w<sub>e</sub> in the same way.

blocks.text: Training puts cross-entropy on the gold start index and on the gold end index. At test time you pick the pair (i, j) with i ≤ j that maximises P_start(i) × P_end(j). The tokens from i to j, joined back into a string, are the answer.
Two numbers score that string. Exact match (EM) compares normalised strings and gives 1 or 0. F1 compares tokens and gives partial credit.

blocks.where: P = overlap ÷ number of predicted tokens; R = overlap ÷ number of gold tokens; overlap is the number of token positions the two answers share; EM = 1 only when the normalised strings are identical, else 0.

sections.h3: Textual entailment: which way does support flow?

blocks.text: Textual entailment, also called natural language inference (NLI), takes a premise and a hypothesis and asks whether a reader who accepts the premise must accept the hypothesis.

There are three labels. Entailment: the hypothesis follows from the premise. Contradiction: the hypothesis cannot be true when the premise is true. Neutral: neither — the premise leaves the question open. SNLI pairs image captions with written hypotheses; MultiNLI does the same with text from several genres.

The model is a sentence-pair classifier. Feed premise and hypothesis through BERT and put a three-way softmax on the [CLS] vector. Stronger designs add cross-attention, so each hypothesis word attends over the premise words and the comparison happens word by word.

Direction matters. The premise entails the hypothesis, not the reverse. "A dog is barking" entails "an animal is making a noise"; the second does not entail the first. Some syllabi call the topic text entailment; the labels are the same.

figure.caption: The predicted answer and the gold answer share only the token cat; the is an extra predicted token. Precision divides that one shared token by two predicted tokens (0.5), recall by one gold token (1.0), giving F1 = 0.667, while exact match stays 0 because the strings differ.

spec.title: Predicted 'the cat' vs gold 'cat'
spec.aria: Token-level comparison of the predicted answer 'the cat' with the gold answer 'cat': one shared token cat, precision 0.5, recall 1.0, F1 0.667, and exact match 0 because the strings differ.

examples.question: A reading-comprehension system returns the span the cat. The gold answer is cat. After normalisation (lower case, punctuation stripped), compute exact match and token-level F1, showing precision and recall.
steps: Tokenise both strings. Gold: [cat] → 1 token. Predicted: [the, cat] → 2 tokens.
Find the overlap of token positions: the token cat appears in both, so overlap = 1.
Check exact match: the strings 'the cat' and 'cat' are not identical, so EM = 0.
examples.answer: EM = 0 and F1 = 0.667, so the system gets no exact-match credit but about two-thirds of the token credit.
examples.check:
from collections import Counter

gold = "cat".split()
pred = "the cat".split()

em = 1 if gold == pred else 0
common = Counter(gold) & Counter(pred)
overlap = sum(common.values())

precision = overlap / len(pred)
recall = overlap / len(gold)
f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)

print(em)
print(round(f1, 3))

traps: EM is 1 only when the normalised strings match exactly; F1 gives partial credit for shared tokens. A system with F1 near 0.8 can still have a much lower EM. Report both and never call either one 'accuracy'.

Entailment is one-directional. Read the arrow from premise to hypothesis. 'A dog is barking' entails 'an animal is making a noise', but the reverse fails, and the reverse pair is not a contradiction either.

Neutral is not contradiction. If the premise does not entail the hypothesis, the pair may still be perfectly consistent. 'A man is playing guitar' and 'A man is playing a musical instrument' are compatible, so the label is entailment, not neutral; pick neutral only when the premise genuinely leaves it open.

In extractive QA the answer must be a span of the passage: the start index is at or before the end index, both lie inside the passage tokens, and neither is in the question. A model that points into the question has learned the wrong thing.

A generative QA model can answer with words that never occur in the passage. EM and F1 then compare strings, so a correct paraphrase may score 0 EM. Use a human or model-based judgement for generative answers.

quiz.q: In NLI, what are the two inputs called and what are the three labels?
quiz.a: Inputs are the premise and the hypothesis. Labels: entailment (hypothesis follows from the premise), contradiction (hypothesis cannot be true when the premise is true), neutral (neither).

quiz.q: Why is entailment one-directional? Give a pair where one direction holds and the other fails.
quiz.a: The premise carries the evidence; the hypothesis is the claim being tested. 'A dog is barking' entails 'an animal is making a noise', but 'an animal is making a noise' does not guarantee a dog, so the reverse fails. The classifier must be trained and read in the premise → hypothesis direction.

quiz.q: Gold answer: 'new york city'. Predicted answer: 'new york'. Both already normalised. Compute EM and token-level F1.
quiz.a: Predicted tokens = 2, gold tokens = 3, overlap = 2. EM = 0 (strings differ). P = 2/2 = 1.0. R = 2/3 = 0.667. F1 = 2 × 1.0 × 0.667 ÷ 1.667 = 0.8. So EM = 0, F1 = 0.8.

quiz.q: A system reports a pair as 'not entailed'. Explain why you cannot record that as contradiction without more evidence.
quiz.a: 'Not entailed' only says the hypothesis is not guaranteed. The pair may be neutral or it may be contradictory — these are separate labels. Marking every non-entailed pair as contradiction inflates that class and makes the confusion matrix meaningless; you must check whether the premise rules the hypothesis out, as in 'the cat is on the mat' against 'the cat is flying'.

quiz.q: Why does an extractive reader need two score vectors, one for start and one for end, instead of a single label per token?
quiz.a: The answer is a span, so the decision is about two boundary positions, not about each token on its own. Two vectors give one distribution over start positions and one over end positions; multiplying them and taking the best pair with start ≤ end returns the span directly.

quiz.q: An open-domain system must answer a question from 1,000 passages. Describe the two stages of the pipeline and say which stage is trained on labelled answer spans.
quiz.a: Stage 1 is retrieval: score and rank the passages against the question, keep the top k. Stage 2 is reading: run the reader on each kept passage with the question. The reader is the stage trained on labelled answer spans; the retriever is trained on question–passage relevance, often with a ranking loss.

quiz.q: When would you prefer F1 to EM when comparing two QA systems?
quiz.a: When the answer boundary is ambiguous or the answer is long. 'the cat' and 'cat' are both correct to a human, but EM scores the first as 0 while F1 gives 0.667. On long answers many correct predictions differ from gold by a word or two, so EM collapses to near 0 and hides real differences; F1 keeps the graded signal. EM is still reported because it is the stricter, harder-to-game number.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern open-domain QA trains the retriever and the reader jointly, and dense retrievers score passages by vector similarity rather than word overlap. Retrieval-augmented generation attaches a retriever to a generator so the answer can be written from fetched passages instead of memory. NLI models are now used as a check on summarisers and chatbots: a summary sentence that contradicts the source document is caught as a contradiction pair. Adversarial NLI sets show that models latch on to word overlap instead of reasoning, and cross-lingual NLI tests whether the same labels survive translation. Search next for dense passage retrieval, retrieval-augmented generation, and the SNLI and MultiNLI benchmarks.
